units.title: Income and Expenses
units.tip: Income is money you receive. Expenses are money you spend. Understanding both is the foundation of personal finance. The difference between them, called net income or surplus, shows whether you are spending more or less than you earn.

exercises.question: What is income?
exercises.answer: Money you receive from work, investments, or other sources
exercises.explain: Income is any money coming in. Salary from a job, interest from a savings account, or revenue from a business are all income.
choices: Money you receive from work, investments, or other sources
The value of things you own

exercises.question: What is an expense?
exercises.answer: Money you spend on goods, services, or obligations
exercises.explain: An expense is any money going out. Food, rent, transportation, insurance, and entertainment are all expenses.
choices: The cost of something you own
Money you spend on goods, services, or obligations

exercises.question: What do you call the difference between income and expenses?
exercises.answer: Surplus if income exceeds expenses, deficit if expenses exceed income
exercises.explain: If you earn 3000 and spend 2000, you have a 1000 surplus. If you earn 3000 and spend 4000, you have a 1000 deficit.
choices: Profit, regardless of which is larger
Surplus if income exceeds expenses, deficit if expenses exceed income

exercises.question: Why is tracking income and expenses important?
exercises.answer: It shows you where your money goes and whether you have surplus or deficit
exercises.explain: Without tracking, you do not know if you are spending more than you earn or where your money is actually going. Tracking reveals patterns and problems.
choices: It shows you where your money goes and whether you have surplus or deficit

exercises.question: What categories might you track expenses in?
exercises.answer: Housing, food, transportation, entertainment, utilities, and more
exercises.explain: Common expense categories help organize spending. Different people use different categories based on their needs.
choices: All expenses are the same category
Housing, food, transportation, entertainment, utilities, and more

exercises.question: What is gross income?
exercises.answer: Total income before any deductions or taxes
exercises.explain: Gross income is the full amount earned. If a job pays 50000 per year, that is the gross income before deductions.
choices: Total income before any deductions or taxes
Money you keep in the bank

exercises.question: What is net income?
exercises.answer: Gross income minus deductions like taxes and benefits
exercises.explain: Net income is the money you actually receive after deductions. If gross is 50000 and deductions are 10000, net is 40000.
choices: Gross income minus deductions like taxes and benefits

exercises.question: What are common deductions from gross income?
exercises.answer: Taxes, health insurance, retirement contributions
exercises.explain: Employers often deduct taxes and benefits from pay automatically. These reduce gross income to get net income.

exercises.question: If your gross income is 4000 per month and deductions are 800, what is your net income?
exercises.answer: 3200 per month
exercises.explain: Net income = Gross income minus Deductions. 4000 minus 800 equals 3200.

exercises.question: Why is it important to know both gross and net income?
exercises.answer: Gross shows total earning power, net shows actual money available to spend
exercises.explain: You cannot spend your gross income because deductions take part of it first. You can only spend net income. Both numbers are important for different reasons.
choices: Gross shows total earning power, net shows actual money available to spend

units.title: Budgeting Basics
units.tip: A budget is a plan for money. It lists expected income and planned spending. Comparing the two shows whether a plan balances and what each goal would take.

exercises.question: What is a budget?
exercises.answer: A plan showing expected income and planned spending
exercises.explain: A budget lists your income sources and plans how to allocate that money to different categories. It is a forward-looking tool.
choices: A plan showing expected income and planned spending
A list of debts you owe
A record of past spending only

exercises.question: In a simple budget, what must be known before spending can be planned?
exercises.answer: How much money is expected to come in
exercises.explain: A plan for spending starts from the income available. Listing all income sources comes first.
choices: The price of every future purchase
The interest rate on a savings account
How much money is expected to come in

exercises.question: In the usual budgeting order, what comes after listing income?
exercises.answer: Listing and estimating expected expenses in each category
exercises.explain: Next come the anticipated expenses, such as housing, food, and transportation, each with an estimated amount.
choices: Listing and estimating expected expenses in each category
Spending all the income at once
Leaving expenses out of the plan

exercises.question: If your monthly income is 3500 and total planned expenses are 3200, what is your budgeted surplus?
exercises.answer: 300 per month
exercises.explain: Budgeted surplus = Income minus Expenses. 3500 minus 3200 equals 300.

exercises.question: What does a budget show when planned expenses are larger than income?
exercises.answer: A deficit, a gap that must be covered somehow
exercises.explain: When planned spending exceeds income, the difference is a deficit. It can only be closed by spending less, earning more, or drawing on savings or borrowing.
choices: A deficit, a gap that must be covered somehow

exercises.question: What is a fixed expense?
exercises.answer: An expense that is the same amount each month
exercises.explain: Fixed expenses do not change. Rent, insurance, and loan payments are typically fixed because the amount is the same every month.
choices: An expense that is the same amount each month
An expense that changes every month

exercises.question: What is a variable expense?
exercises.answer: An expense that changes from month to month
exercises.explain: Variable expenses fluctuate. Groceries, dining out, and entertainment vary in cost depending on what you buy.
choices: An expense that changes from month to month
An expense that stays the same

exercises.question: Which are typically fixed expenses?
exercises.answer: Rent or mortgage, insurance, loan payments
exercises.explain: These are contracted amounts paid to the same payee each month. You know the exact amount in advance.
choices: Rent or mortgage, insurance, loan payments

exercises.question: Which are typically variable expenses?
exercises.answer: Groceries, entertainment, clothing, dining out
exercises.explain: These amounts change based on what you buy and how much you choose to spend. They are harder to predict exactly.

exercises.question: Why do budgets treat fixed and variable expenses differently?
exercises.answer: Fixed amounts are known in advance, variable amounts must be estimated
exercises.explain: Fixed expenses repeat at the same amount, so they are easy to plan. Variable expenses change, so a budget uses an estimate for them.
choices: Fixed expenses never have to be paid
Fixed amounts are known in advance, variable amounts must be estimated

units.title: Saving and Emergency Funds
units.tip: Saving is spending less than is earned and setting the difference aside. An emergency fund is savings set aside for unexpected costs such as a medical bill or loss of income. Its purpose is to absorb financial shocks.

exercises.question: What is saving?
exercises.answer: Spending less than you earn and setting money aside
exercises.explain: Saving is the act of not spending all your income. The unspent money is set aside for future use.
choices: Spending less than you earn and setting money aside

exercises.question: What can savings be used for?
exercises.answer: Meeting future goals and absorbing unexpected expenses
exercises.explain: Savings can fund planned goals or cover surprise costs without borrowing.
choices: Replacing the need for any income
Meeting future goals and absorbing unexpected expenses

exercises.question: If your monthly surplus is 300, how much would you save in a year?
exercises.explain: Savings per year = Monthly surplus times 12. 300 times 12 equals 3600.

exercises.question: Why do some people keep savings in an account separate from spending money?
exercises.answer: Separation makes the money less tempting to spend
exercises.explain: Money kept apart from everyday spending is less likely to be used for routine purchases.
choices: Separation makes the money less tempting to spend
It is the only way to save

exercises.question: What is 'paying yourself first'?
exercises.answer: Setting aside savings before paying other expenses
exercises.explain: Instead of saving what is left after spending, decide on a savings amount first and spend what remains. This prioritizes saving.
choices: Setting aside savings before paying other expenses

exercises.question: What is an emergency fund?
exercises.answer: Money set aside specifically for unexpected expenses
exercises.explain: An emergency fund is savings reserved for unexpected costs like medical bills, car repairs, or loss of income. It is often kept apart from other savings.
choices: Money set aside specifically for unexpected expenses

exercises.question: Why do people often keep an emergency fund separate from other savings?
exercises.answer: To make it harder to spend on non-emergencies
exercises.explain: A separate fund is less likely to be used for routine purchases, which keeps it available for true emergencies.
choices: It always earns more interest there
To make it harder to spend on non-emergencies

exercises.question: How is the size of an emergency fund usually described?
exercises.answer: In months of essential living expenses
exercises.explain: Funds are often sized as a number of months of essential expenses. The right number depends on a person's situation, so it is not a single fixed target.
choices: By the number of bank accounts held
In months of essential living expenses
As a fixed amount that is the same for everyone

exercises.question: If essential expenses are 2500 a month, how much does a fund covering four months of them hold?
exercises.explain: Four months of 2500 is 4 times 2500, which equals 10000.

exercises.question: After an emergency fund has been used, what is true until it is refilled?
exercises.answer: It is smaller, so it protects against less
exercises.explain: An emergency fund only protects up to the amount in it. Once money is withdrawn, there is less available for the next emergency.
choices: It has turned into a loan
It is smaller, so it protects against less

units.title: Simple and Compound Interest
units.tip: Interest is the cost of borrowing money or the reward for lending it. Simple interest is calculated on the principal only. Compound interest is calculated on principal plus accumulated interest, making it grow faster.

exercises.question: What is interest?
exercises.answer: The cost of borrowing money or the reward for saving it
exercises.explain: When you borrow, you pay interest. When you save or invest, you earn interest. Interest is the price of money over time.
choices: A fee for using a bank
The cost of borrowing money or the reward for saving it
The total amount of a loan

exercises.question: What does an interest rate tell you?
exercises.answer: The percentage of the principal charged or earned over a period, usually a year
exercises.explain: A rate of 5 percent per year means 5 percent of the principal is charged or earned each year. A higher rate means more interest on the same principal.
choices: The percentage of the principal charged or earned over a period, usually a year
How much total money is owed

exercises.question: What is the principal?
exercises.answer: The original amount of money borrowed or invested
exercises.explain: If you borrow 10000, the principal is 10000. Interest is calculated based on this principal.
choices: The original amount of money borrowed or invested

exercises.question: On the same principal, what does doubling the simple interest rate do to the interest per year?
exercises.answer: It doubles the interest
exercises.explain: On 1000 at 3 percent simple interest, the interest is 30 per year. At 6 percent it is 60 per year. Double the rate means double the interest.

exercises.question: What does it mean if a savings account pays interest?
exercises.answer: The bank gives you money as a reward for keeping your money there
exercises.explain: Banks that pay interest on savings do so because they lend out deposited money. The depositor earns a return on the balance held.
choices: The bank charges you a fee
You have to pay to keep money there
The bank gives you money as a reward for keeping your money there

exercises.question: What is simple interest?
exercises.answer: Interest calculated only on the principal, not on accumulated interest
exercises.explain: With simple interest, interest is calculated on the original amount only. Each year you earn the same amount of interest.
choices: Interest calculated only on the principal, not on accumulated interest

exercises.question: If you invest 1000 at 5 percent simple interest, how much interest do you earn in year one?
exercises.explain: Simple interest = Principal times Rate. 1000 times 0.05 equals 50.

exercises.question: What is compound interest?
exercises.answer: Interest calculated on principal plus previously earned interest
exercises.explain: With compound interest, interest earns interest. Each year, you calculate interest on a larger amount (principal plus accumulated interest).
choices: Interest calculated on principal plus previously earned interest

exercises.question: If you invest 1000 at 5 percent compound interest (compounded annually), how much is it worth after 2 years?
exercises.explain: Year 1: 1000 plus 50 interest equals 1050. Year 2: 1050 times 0.05 equals 52.50 interest. 1050 plus 52.50 equals 1102.50.

exercises.question: Why does compound interest grow faster than simple interest?
exercises.answer: Interest earns its own interest, creating exponential growth
exercises.explain: With compound interest, the growing total earns interest each period. Simple interest earns only on the original amount. Over time, compound interest creates much larger growth.
choices: Compound interest is the same as simple
Interest earns its own interest, creating exponential growth

units.title: Debt and Credit Scores
units.tip: Debt is money owed to others. Borrowing has a cost in the form of interest. A credit score is a number that summarizes how reliably someone has repaid borrowed money.

exercises.question: What is debt?
exercises.answer: Money you owe to others that must be repaid
exercises.explain: Debt is an obligation to repay borrowed money. Credit card balances, loans, and mortgages are all debt.
choices: Money you owe to others that must be repaid

exercises.question: What is a loan?
exercises.answer: A fixed amount of money you borrow and agree to repay with interest
exercises.explain: A loan is a formal agreement where you borrow a specific amount and must repay it in regular payments, usually including interest.
choices: Free money given by a bank
A fixed amount of money you borrow and agree to repay with interest

exercises.question: What is a credit card?
exercises.answer: A card that lets you borrow money up to a limit, which you must repay
exercises.explain: A credit card allows you to borrow money for purchases. You receive a bill and must repay the amount used, plus interest if you do not pay in full.
choices: A way to earn free money
A card that lets you borrow money up to a limit, which you must repay

exercises.question: Why can credit card debt become expensive?
exercises.answer: Interest builds on any balance that is not paid in full
exercises.explain: If only part of the balance is paid, the unpaid amount accrues interest, which adds to what is owed.
choices: Paying in full adds extra interest
Cards cannot be used to buy things
Interest builds on any balance that is not paid in full

exercises.question: What can a record of on-time repayment do?
exercises.answer: Build a credit history that lenders can review
exercises.explain: Borrowing and repaying on time shows lenders a pattern of reliability. It can influence whether and on what terms they lend later, but it guarantees nothing.
choices: Build a credit history that lenders can review

exercises.question: What is a credit score?
exercises.answer: A number that measures how reliably you repay borrowed money
exercises.explain: A credit score summarizes your borrowing and repayment history. Lenders use it to decide whether to lend to you and what interest rate to offer.
choices: The amount of money you have
A number that measures how reliably you repay borrowed money

exercises.question: What kinds of information do credit scores typically draw on?
exercises.answer: Payment history, amount owed, length of credit history, new credit
exercises.explain: Credit scores typically draw on whether payments are made on time, how much is owed compared to limits, how long credit has been used, and how much new credit was recently sought. Details differ between scoring systems.
choices: Payment history, amount owed, length of credit history, new credit

exercises.question: What does a higher credit score mean?
exercises.answer: Lenders see you as a lower risk and more likely to approve your loans
exercises.explain: A high credit score shows you reliably repay debts. Lenders trust you more and may offer better interest rates.
choices: Lenders see you as a lower risk and more likely to approve your loans

exercises.question: What hurts your credit score?
exercises.answer: Late payments, high debt levels, defaulting on loans
exercises.explain: Missing payments, carrying large balances, and failing to repay loans all damage your credit score.
choices: Late payments, high debt levels, defaulting on loans

exercises.question: Which behaviors do credit scores generally reward?
exercises.answer: Paying on time and keeping balances low relative to limits
exercises.explain: Consistent on-time payments and moderate balances are the patterns scoring systems generally read as reliable.
choices: Paying on time and keeping balances low relative to limits
Borrowing the maximum on every account

units.title: Insurance and Needs vs Wants
units.tip: Insurance is protection against financial risk. Insurance pools risk across many people so that individuals are protected from large unexpected costs. Needs are essential items and expenses. Wants are things you desire but could live without.

exercises.question: What is insurance?
exercises.answer: A way to protect yourself financially against unexpected losses or expenses
exercises.explain: Insurance is an agreement where you pay a regular premium (fee) and the insurance company reimburses you for covered losses or expenses.
choices: A way to earn free money
A way to protect yourself financially against unexpected losses or expenses

exercises.question: What is a premium in insurance?
exercises.answer: The regular payment you make to maintain insurance coverage
exercises.explain: A premium is the cost of insurance. You might pay a monthly or annual premium to keep your insurance policy active.
choices: The regular payment you make to maintain insurance coverage
The amount the insurance company keeps

exercises.question: What is a deductible in insurance?
exercises.answer: The amount you must pay before the insurance company pays for a loss
exercises.explain: If your deductible is 500 and you have a 2000 loss, you pay 500 and insurance pays 1500.
choices: A fee for making a claim
Money the insurance company pays you
The amount you must pay before the insurance company pays for a loss

exercises.question: What does health insurance spread across many people?
exercises.answer: Large, unpredictable medical costs
exercises.explain: Medical care can be very expensive and hard to predict. Insurance pools the risk so that the cost of a rare large event is shared.
choices: Ordinary predictable expenses such as rent

exercises.question: How does insurance risk pooling work?
exercises.answer: Many people pay premiums so that some who experience losses are covered
exercises.explain: Insurance companies collect premiums from thousands of people. Most never make a claim, but those who do are protected. This spreads risk across the group.
choices: Many people pay premiums so that some who experience losses are covered

exercises.question: What is a need?
exercises.answer: An essential item or expense required for basic living
exercises.explain: Needs are things you must have to survive and function. Food, housing, utilities, and clothing are needs.
choices: An essential item or expense required for basic living
Something you want but cannot afford

exercises.question: What is a want?
exercises.answer: Something you desire but could live without
exercises.explain: Wants are things you like but are not necessary. Entertainment, dining out, and luxury items are wants.
choices: Something you desire but could live without

exercises.question: Which of these is a need?
exercises.answer: Shelter (housing)
exercises.explain: Shelter is essential for survival. Entertainment, vacations, and luxury goods are wants, not needs.

exercises.question: Which of these is a want?
exercises.answer: Dining out at restaurants
exercises.explain: Dining out is enjoyable but not necessary. You could cook at home. Basic food is a need, but restaurant dining is a want.

exercises.question: In a needs-first budgeting approach, what is covered first?
exercises.answer: Needs, then wants from what remains
exercises.explain: Covering essentials first means the remaining money is what is available for wants.
choices: Wants, then needs from what remains
Needs, then wants from what remains
